parole.significato: abacist (one who calculates using an abacus)

From Late Latin ancra, angra (“valley, space between two trees”), perhaps a variant of Vulgar Latin *angula, from Latin angulus (“angle, corner”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese cobertura, from Late Latin coopertūra, from Latin coopertus.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cobiiça, from Late Latin *cupiditia, from Latin cupiditātem (“desire, greed”). Cognate with Galician cobiza and Spanish codicia.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Late Latin cuprum (“copper”), from Latin cyprium (aes) (“Cypriot copper”), from Ancient Greek Κύπρος (Kúpros), because Cyprus was its chief source.
Uncertain. Possibly from Late Latin coccum (“kernel, seed”), from Ancient Greek κόκκος (kókkos). Doublet of coque.
From Late Latin cofia, of West Germanic origin. See also Middle High German kupfe (“cap”), Old High German kupphia (“cap”), all from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰeybʰ-.
Inherited from Late Latin collāre, from Latin collāris + -āre.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese colhon, from Late Latin cōleōnem, from Latin cōleus (“sack, scrotum”). Cognate with Galician collón, Spanish cojón, Catalan colló.
From Late Latin collīna, possibly through French colline or Italian collina, From the feminine of Latin collīnus, from collis (“hill”), from Proto-Indo-European *kl̥Hnís (“hill”), from *kelH-.

From Late Latin commāter, from com- (“together”) + māter (“mother”). Cognate with Catalan and Italian comare, Neapolitan cummà, Sicilian cummari, Galician and Spanish comadre, French commère, Norman conméthe, Romanian cumătră.
Borrowed from Late Latin combīnāre.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin combīnātiōnem. By surface analysis, combinar + -ção.
Borrowed from Late Latin commerciālis. By surface analysis, comércio + -al.

parole.significato: to deal, to trade; to do business
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin commerciārī. By surface analysis, comércio + -ar.

parole.significato: itch (a sensation felt on an area of the skin that causes a person or animal to want to scratch)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin comestiōnem, from Latin comestus. Compare Galician comechón and Spanish comezón.

parole.significato: godfather of one’s child; father of one’s godchild
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese compadre, conpadre, from Late Latin compatrem, from com- + Latin pater. Cognate with Galician and Spanish compadre, Catalan and Italian compare.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin competītiōnem, from Latin competō. By surface analysis, competir + -ção.
Borrowed from Late Latin competentia. By surface analysis, competir + -ência.
Borrowed from Late Latin compīlātōrem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin comprehēnsīvus.
Borrowed from Late Latin compulsāre, from Latin compulsus.
Borrowed from Late Latin compulsiōnem, from Latin compulsus.
Borrowed from Late Latin compūnctiōnem.
From Late Latin commūnālis, from Latin commūnis.
From Late Latin concīsus (“cut short”), from Latin concīdō (“to cut to pieces”), from com- + caedō (“to cut, to strike down”), from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂id-, *kh₂eyd- (“to cut, hew”).
From Late Latin conclūsīvus, from Latin conclūsīvē (“conclusively”), from past participle of conclūdō. By surface analysis, concluso + -ivo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Late Latin cōnsacrāre, from Latin cōnsecrāre.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin cōnstēllātiōnem.
From Late Latin cōnstrūctōrem (“builder”), from Latin cōnstruere (“to build, pile together”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin cōnsuētūdinārius. Piecewise doublet of costumeiro.

parole.significato: contagious (of a disease, able to be transmitted to others)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin contāgiōsus. By surface analysis, contágio (“contagion”) + -oso.

parole.significato: tale, story (account of an asserted fact or circumstance)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese conto, from Vulgar Latin *contu(s), *comptu(s), from Latin computus (“calculation”). Doublet of cômputo.
Borrowed from Late Latin contrādictōrius (“contradictory”), from Latin contrādīcō (“to speak against; to contradict”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin cooperātor. By surface analysis, cooperar + -dor.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin cooperātīvus. By surface analysis, cooperar + -tivo.
From Late Latin *cuppu, from Late Latin cūppa, from Latin cūpa.

parole.significato: coral (any of various species of anthozoans)
parole.testo: From Late Latin corallum or Latin corallium, from Ancient Greek κοράλλιον (korállion, “coral”), of uncertain origin.
From Late Latin corporātiō (“assumption of a body”), from Latin corporātus, past participle of corporāre (“to form into a body”)

parole.significato: curtain (piece of cloth covering a window)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cortina~cortinha, from Late Latin cōrtīna (“curtain”).

parole.significato: any piece of armour made of leather
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin coriācea (vestis), from coriāceus, from Latin corium. Compare French cuirasse, source of English cuirass.

parole.significato: thigh (part of the leg above the knee)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese coixa, from Late Latin coxa (“thigh”), from Proto-Italic *koksā, from Proto-Indo-European *kóḱseh₂, from *koḱs- (“joint, limb”) + *-eh₂.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cozer, from Late Latin cocēre, from Latin coquere, from Proto-Italic *kʷekʷō, from Proto-Indo-European *pekʷ- (“to cook, become ripe”). Compare Galician cocer.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cozinha, from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna. Compare Galician cociña, Asturian and Spanish cocina, French cuisine.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cozinnar, from Late Latin cocīnāre, from Latin coquīnāre. Compare Galician cociñar, Spanish cocinar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese creença, from Late Latin crēdentia, from Latin crēdēns. By surface analysis, crer + -ença. Doublet of credência and credença.

parole.significato: criminal (of or relating to crime or penal law)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin or Juridical Latin criminālis (“criminal”), from Latin crīmen (“verdict; crime”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin Chrīstiānitātem, from Latin Chrīstiānus (“Christian”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese crivar, from Late Latin or Vulgar Latin cribāre, a dissimilated form of Latin cribrāre.
From Late Latin or Vulgar Latin cribum, dissimilated form of Latin cribrum attested in some late glosses.

parole.significato: to crucify (to execute a person by nailing to a crucifix)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese crucifigar, from Late Latin crucificāre, from Latin crucifigō. By surface analysis, cruz + -ificar.
From Late Latin crucifīxiō.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cuco, from Late Latin cucus or cuccus, or Latin cuculus or Ancient Greek κόκκυξ (kókkux).
From Old Galician-Portuguese cardeo, earlier cardẽo, from Late Latin cardinus, from carduus (“thistle”).
Borrowed from Late Latin complicem (“confederate, participant”), from Latin complicō (“to fold together”). Compare English accomplice.

parole.significato: date (point of time at which a transaction or event takes place)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin data, from Latin datus (“given”). Doublet of dado and dada.
Borrowed from Late Latin decānus, from Latin decem (“ten”). Doublet of deão, which was borrowed from Old French.

parole.significato: to behead; to decapitate (remove the head of)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin decapitāre, from dē- + caput (“head”) + -āre.

parole.significato: decimal (concerning numbers expressed in decimal or calculations using decimal)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin decimālis, from Latin decimus. By surface analysis, décimo + -al.
Borrowed from Late Latin dēclārātīvus.

parole.significato: thimble (cap for the fingers, used in sewing to push the needle)
parole.testo: From Late Latin digitāle, from Latin digitālis (“digital”), from digitus. By surface analysis, dedo + -al. Doublet of digital.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēfectīvus.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese defesa, from Late Latin dēfēnsa (“defence”). Doublet of defensa and devesa.
Borrowed from Late Latin dēficientia, from Latin dēficiēns. Compare Catalan deficiència, French déficience, Italian deficienza, Spanish deficiencia.
Borrowed from Late Latin deificāre (“to make a god, to deify”), from Latin deus (“god”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēlinquentia (compare Catalan delinqüència, Spanish delincuencia), from Latin dēlinquēns. By surface analysis, delinquir + -ência.
From Old Galician-Portuguese dentro, from Late Latin dē intrō.
From Old Galician-Portuguese descalçar, from Late Latin discalceāre, from Latin calceāre. Cognate with Galician and Spanish descalzar, French déchausser, Italian discalzare and Romanian descălța.

parole.significato: to unload (unload cargo, wares, etc from a vehicle)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese descarregar, from Late Latin discarricāre (“to unload”), from carricō (“to load”), from Latin carrus (“car, wagon”). By surface analysis, des- + carregar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese descoberto, from Late Latin discoopertus, from Latin dis- + coopertus.

parole.significato: to discover (to find something for the first time)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese descobrir (“to find out”), from Late Latin discoperīre < discooperīre (“to expose”), from Latin dis- + cooperiō (“to cover wholly”). By surface analysis, des- + cobrir.

parole.significato: desertion (act of leaving one’s duty or post)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin dēsertiōnem, from Latin dēsertus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese despesa, despensa, from Late Latin dispensa, from Latin dispendere. Doublet of despesa and dispensa.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese despesa, from Late Latin dispēnsa. Doublet of despensa and dispensa.
From Late Latin dēstrūctor.
Inherited from Late Latin dē trāns.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēvāstātiōnem. By surface analysis, devastar + -ção.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese devesa, from Late Latin [terra] dēfēnsa (“defended land”). Cognate with Galician devesa and Spanish dehesa. Doublet of defesa and defensa.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin diaphorēticus, from Ancient Greek διαφορητικός (diaphorētikós).

Borrowed from Late Latin diamantem, from Latin adamantem, from Ancient Greek ἀδάμᾱς (adámās, “invincible, untamed; hard substance”), from ἀ- (a-, “un-”) + δαμάζω (damázō, “to overpower, tame, conquer”), from Proto-Indo-European *demh₂-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese deante, from de + enante. Enante from Late Latin in ante, from Latin in ante. Cognate with Galician diante, Asturian, Leonese, and Mirandese delantre and Spanish delante.
Borrowed from Late Latin diarrhoea, from Ancient Greek διάρροια (diárrhoia, “through-flowing”), from διά (diá, “through”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dīgestīvus.
Semi-learned form modified from the earlier director, borrowed from Late Latin dīrēctōrem, from Latin dīrēctus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin discrētiōnem.
Borrowed from Late Latin diūrēticus, from Ancient Greek διουρητικός (diourētikós), from διουρέω (diouréō, “to pass urine, have diuretic properties”).
Borrowed from Late Latin divisibilis, from the verb Latin dividō.
Inherited from Late Latin dūplāre, from Latin dūplus. Compare Spanish doblar, French doubler, Italian doppiare. Doublet of dublar.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dolōrōsus (“painful”), from Latin dolor (“pain; grief”) + -ōsus (“-ous”). Displaced the inherited Old Galician-Portuguese dooroso.

From Old Galician-Portuguese dom, don, from Late Latin domnus, a syncopated form of Latin dominus (“lord, master”). The Latin form survived in ecclesiastical usage, evolving in Old Portuguese (and Western Romance) via cluster simplification from -mn- to -m-/-n-, with dom standardizing in Portuguese
Borrowed from Late Latin domātōrem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dominātiōnem. By surface analysis, dominar + -ção.
From Old Galician-Portuguese domingo, from a shortening of Late Latin diēs Dominicus (“Sunday”, literally “day of the Lord”). Doublet of domínico, which is a borrowing.

parole.significato: Dominican (relating to St. Dominic or his religious order)
parole.testo: From Late Latin Dominicus + -ano.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dono, from Late Latin domnus, from Latin dominus (“lord”), from domus (“house”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dṓm (“house”), from *dem- (“to build”). Compare Galician dono and Spanish dueño. Doublet of Dom and dominó.
From Old Galician-Portuguese dourar, from Late Latin dēaurāre (“to gild”), from Latin aurāre.
From Late Latin drāma, from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma, “an act, a theatrical act, a play”). Doublet of dorama.
From Late Latin drāmaticus, from Ancient Greek δραματικός (dramatikós).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dromedārius (“kind of camel”), from Latin *dromadārius, from dromas, dromadis (“dromedary”) + -ārius (suffix forming nouns denoting agents of use).

parole.significato: duality (a classification into two subclasses or opposed parts).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin duālitās.
Inherited from Late Latin dē ex.
From Late Latin diptycha, plural, from Ancient Greek, neuter plural of δίπτυχος (díptukhos, “folded, doubled”), from δι (di) + -πτυχος (-ptukhos) (akin to Greek πτυχή (ptychí, “fold, layer”)).

parole.significato: pity (feeling of sympathy at the misfortune or suffering of someone or something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese doo, from Late Latin dolus, from Latin dolor (“pain”). Compare Spanish duelo.
Borrowed from Late Latin ecclēsiasticus (“of the church”), from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησιαστικός (ekklēsiastikós), from ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía).

parole.significato: ecumenical (pertaining to the Christian Church worldwide)
parole.testo: From Late Latin oecūmenicus, from Ancient Greek οἰκουμενικός (oikoumenikós).

parole.significato: edible (that can be eaten without harm)
parole.testo: From Late Latin edibilis, from Latin edō (“to eat”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin elenchus, from Ancient Greek ἔλεγχος (élenkhos). Compare Italian and Spanish elenco.

parole.significato: to become leaner; to lose body weight
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese enmagrecer, from Late Latin ēmacrēscere, from Latin macer (“lean”), from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós. By surface analysis, e- + magro + -ecer.

parole.significato: to rock (move gently back and forth)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibilities include: * From abalar. * From Late Latin ballāre (“to play, dance”), prefixed with em-.

parole.significato: to ambush (to lie in wait for, or to attack)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin imboscāre, from Frankish *busk (“bush”), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“bush, thicket”).
From Late Latin imbūtum, from trāiectōrium imbutum, perhaps through Occitan. Cognate with Galician embude, Asturian embudu and Spanish embudo.
Borrowed from Late Latin ēmigrātiōnem, from Latin ēmigrō (“to emigrate”).
Inherited from Late Latin *impignāre, from pignus (“pledge”). Compare Spanish empeñar and Italian impegnare.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese empuxar /enpuxar (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Late Latin impulsāre, from in- + pulsāre, or a frequentative of impellere. Doublet of impulsar, a learned borrowing, and possibly of empurrar. Cognate with Galician empuxar, Spanish empujar.
From Late Latin encliticus, from Ancient Greek ἐγκλιτικός (enklitikós).
Inherited from Late Latin *entubus, from Latin intŭbus.

parole.significato: to get or cause someone to get disgusted or nauseated
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese anojar~enojar, from Late Latin inodiāre. Doublet of anojar and enojar. Compare Galician anoxar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese *eisaio, from Late Latin exagium, from Latin exigō.
Borrowed from Late Latin entelechīa, from Ancient Greek ἐντελέχεια (entelékheia).

Borrowed from Late Latin enthūsiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós, “inspiration, enthusiasm”), from ἔνθεος (éntheos, “possessed by a god”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + θεός (theós, “god”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese enviar, from Late Latin inviāre, from Latin via (“path, road”). Compare Spanish and Catalan enviar, French envoyer, Italian inviare.
From Late Latin asciola, from Latin ascia. Compare Galician aixola, Spanish azuela.

parole.significato: epicycle (a small circle whose centre is on the circumference of a larger circle)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin epicy̆clus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίκυκλος (epíkuklos). By surface analysis, epi- + ciclo.
Borrowed from Late Latin episcopālis.
Borrowed from Late Latin epistola, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ).
From Late Latin aequivocāre. Cognate with English equivocate.
From Late Latin aequivocus (“equivocal, ambiguous”).

parole.significato: era (time period of indeterminate length, generally more than one year)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin aera.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ermo, hermo, from Late Latin eremus, from Latin erēmus, from Ancient Greek ἔρημος (érēmos), with preservation of Greek accent over vowel length in Late Latin. Compare Aromanian ermu

parole.significato: of, from or relating to Santarém, Portugal
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin scalabitānus, from Latin Scalabis.
From Late Latin excaldāre, from Latin cal(i)dus (“hot”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin scandalizō, from Ancient Greek σκανδαλίζω (skandalízō). By surface analysis, escândalo + -izar.

parole.significato: to mock; to make fun of
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese escarnir, from Late Latin *scarnīre, *scernīre, possibly through an Old French or Old Occitan intermediary.
From Late Latin scholāris, from Latin schola.
From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Late Latin scōpāre (“to brush or sweep away”), from Latin scōpae (“broom”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese escudeiro, escudeyro, from Late Latin scūtārius, from Latin scūtum. By surface analysis, escudo + -eiro.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin sphēra, from Latin sphaera, borrowed from Ancient Greek σφαῖρᾰ (sphaîră, “ball, globe”).

parole.significato: alms (small amount of money or goods given to someone as charity)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese esmolla, esmolna, earlier elmosna, from Late Latin eleēmosyna, from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē).
Borrowed from Late Latin speciālitātem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin specificāre. By surface analysis, específico + -ar or espécie + -ificar.
Borrowed from Late Latin speculātīvus, from Latin speculor. By surface analysis, especular + -tivo.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin speculātiōnem, from Latin speculor. By surface analysis, especular + -ção. Compare Galician especulación.
Borrowed from Late Latin specificus, from speciēs (“kind”) + faciō (“make”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin spīrituālis. By surface analysis, espírito + -ual.
From Late Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπόρος (spóros, “sowing”) and σπείρω (speírō, “to sow”), from Proto-Indo-European *sper- (“to strew”).

parole.significato: spatula (kitchen utensil for turning and lifting)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin spatula, from Latin spatha. Compare the semi-learned doublet espádua and inherited doublet espalda.
Borrowed from Late Latin essentiālis, from Latin essentia (“being, essence”). By surface analysis, essência + -al.
From Late Latin stēla (“star”), from Latin stēlla.
From Old Galician-Portuguese estrada, strada, from Late Latin strāta (“paved road”), from Latin [via] strāta, feminine of strātus.
From Late Latin stupendus (“stunning, amazing”), from the verb stupeō (“(I) am stunned”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese eu, from Late Latin eo, from Classical Latin egō̆. Doublet of ego.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin evangelismus. By surface analysis, evangelho + -ismo.

parole.significato: to evangelize (preach the Christian gospel, especially to non-Christians)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ēvangelizāre, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: evasion (the act of eluding or avoiding)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ēvāsiōnem, from Latin ēvādō.
Borrowed from Late Latin ēvictiōnem, from Latin ēvincō.
Inherited from Late Latin excommunicō (“put out of the community”).
Borrowed from Late Latin excrētiōnem, from Latin excernō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin existentia.

parole.significato: extortion (the practice of extorting money or other property)
parole.testo: From Late Latin extortiō, from extorqueō.
From Old Galician-Portuguese falcon, from Late Latin falcōnem, probably of Germanic origin.
From Old Galician-Portuguese falsidade, falssidade, from Late Latin falsitātem. By surface analysis, falso + -idade.

parole.significato: to falsify (to alter so as to be false)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin falsificāre (“to make false, to corrupt, to counterfeit, to falsify”), from Latin falsificus, from falsus (“false”). By surface analysis, falso + -ificar.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese faraó, faraón, from Late Latin Pharaōnem, from Ancient Greek Φαραώ (Pharaṓ), from Hebrew פַּרְעֹה (par‘ōh), from Egyptian pr:aA (pr-ꜥꜣ, “palace, pharaoh”), from pr (“house”) + ꜥꜣ (“big”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese feira, from Late Latin feria (“festival, holiday”), from Latin feriae, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁s (“god, godhead, deity”). Cognate with Galician feira, Spanish feria, French foire, Italian fiera, Sicilian fera and English fair. Doublet of féria
Borrowed from Late Latin fēlīcitāre.

parole.significato: down (protruding hair from upholstery or fabric)
parole.testo: From Late Latin faluppa, through Old French felpe, perhaps ultimately of Germanic origin and borrowed from Frankish *felt. Compare Italian and Spanish felpa, and Sicilian ferpa.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin phaenomenon, from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing appearing to view”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese festa, from Late Latin fēsta, from the plural of Latin fēstum.

From Old Galician-Portuguese fevereiro, fevreyro, febreyro, from Late Latin Febrārius, from Latin Februārius, from fēbruum (“purification”), via the purification ritual Fēbrua held on February 15 in the old Roman calendar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fiar, from Late Latin fīlāre, from Latin fīlum. Derivable from fio + -ar. Compare Galician fiar, Spanish hilar.
Borrowed from Late Latin figūrātīvus.

parole.significato: philanthropy (benevolent altruism with the intention of increasing the well-being of mankind)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin philanthrōpia, from Ancient Greek φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpía).
Borrowed from Late Latin fīnālis, from fīnis. By surface analysis, fim + -al.

parole.significato: Finnish (of or relating to Finland or Finns)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin Finnus, from Proto-Germanic *finnaz.
From Late Latin physiologicus, from Ancient Greek φυσιολογικός (phusiologikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin physiognōmia, from Ancient Greek φυσιογνωμία (phusiognōmía, “physiology”), from φύσις (phúsis, “physique, appearance”) + γνώμη (gnṓmē, “means of knowing”).

parole.significato: to flower; to blossom (to put forth blooms)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin flōrīre, from Latin flōrēre. Doublet of chorir, a dialectal inherited term.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin fluentia. By surface analysis, fluir + -ência.

parole.significato: a type of sweet and spongy cake or bread
parole.testo: From Late Latin focācium (via its plural focācia), derived from Latin focus (“hearth”). Compare Galician fogaza, Spanish hogaza and Italian foccacia.
From Old Galician-Portuguese fogueira, fogueyra, from Late Latin, Vulgar Latin *focāria, from focārius ("of a hearth"), from Latin focus (“(controlled) fire”). Compare Spanish hoguera.
From Late Latin follicāre (“to pant, to blow, to breathe”), from Latin follis (“bellows”). Compare Spanish holgar. Doublet of folgar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese folgar, from Late Latin follicāre (“to pant, to blow, to breathe”), from Latin follis (“bellows”). Doublet of folegar.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese folla, from Late Latin folia, from the plural of folium, probably from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolh₃yom (“leaf”), from *bʰleh₃- (“blossom, flower”). Compare Galician folla and Spanish hoja.

parole.significato: foliate; foliar (of or relating to leaves)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Late Latin folia.
Borrowed from Late Latin fōmentāre.

parole.significato: to fortify; to strengthen (to make stronger)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin fortificāre, from Latin fortis. By surface analysis, forte + -ificar.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin fortificātiōnem. By surface analysis, fortificar + -ção.

From Old Galician-Portuguese força, from Late Latin fortia, a noun derived from the neuter plural of Latin fortis (“strong”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“fort”). Compare Galician forza, Spanish fuerza.

Altered from earlier frângão, of unknown origin. Possibly from Late Latin franganus, perhaps a popular or remodeled formation connected with Latin fringilla (“small bird”), with nasal variation or deformation of the stem, though the phonological development is irregular and uncertain. First attested

From Late Latin flascō (with a different outcome from the most common inherited outcome in ch-), from Frankish *flaska (“bottle, flask”), from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ (“bottle, flask”). Doublet of fiasco.

parole.significato: phrase (a short written or spoken expression)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fruita, from Late Latin fructa, designating the collective of Latin frūctus. Compare Galician froita.

parole.significato: funeral (ceremony to honour and bury a deceased person)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin fūnerālis, from Latin funus.
Borrowed from Late Latin fūnerārius, from Latin funus.

From Old Galician-Portuguese foron, from Late Latin fūrōnem (“thief”), from Classical Latin fūr (“thief”), from Proto-Italic *fōr (“thief”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰṓr (“thief”), which is derived from *bʰer- (“to carry”). Cognate with Galician furón, Spanish hurón, Catalan and Occitan fura, Fren

parole.significato: to flog, whip, lash, beat with force
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin fūstīgāre, from Latin fūstis.

parole.significato: a wage paid weekly or every fifteen days
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin feria < Latin feriae. Compare the doublet feira.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Late Latin fīcātum (“liver”), from Latin iecur fīcātum (“fig-stuffed liver”). Compare Spanish hígado, Italian fegato.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin fimbria, from Latin fimbriae. Doublet of franja.

parole.significato: jay (any bird of the genus Garrulus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin gaius.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Late Latin caveola, diminutive from Latin cavea. Cognate to Spanish gayola. Compare jaula, a doublet borrowed through French.
From Old Galician-Portuguese gata, from Late Latin catta.
From Old Galician-Portuguese gato, from Late Latin cattum; compare also catta, possibly of ultimately Afroasiatic origin. See the etymology at cat for further details.

parole.significato: genealogy (the descent of a person, family, or group from an ancestor or ancestors)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin geneālogia, from Ancient Greek γενεᾱλογία (geneālogía), from γενεά (geneá, “generation, descent”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”).
Borrowed from Late Latin gibbōsus, from Latin gibbus (“hump”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin glōssa, from Ancient Greek γλῶσσᾰ (glôssă).
Inherited from Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi).
Inherited from Late Latin grassus. Influenced by graxa. Doublet of crasso.
Borrowed from Late Latin Graecitātem (“Greek language”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin granulum, diminutive of Latin granum (“grain”).
From Late Latin gabia, from Latin cavea. Doublet of the inherited gaiva.

parole.significato: Gothic (an extinct Germanic language, once spoken by the Goths)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin gothicus (“gothic”).
Borrowed from Late Latin habituāre.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese arpa, from Late Latin harpa, from Frankish *harpā, from Proto-Germanic *harpǭ.

Learned borrowing from Late Latin heteroclitus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερόκλιτος (heteróklitos), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + κλίνω (klínō, “lean, incline”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley-.
Borrowed from Late Latin hypnōticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “inducing sleep”, “soporific”).

Borrowed from Late Latin hypochondriacus (“pertaining to or affecting the belly”), from Ancient Greek ὑποχονδριακός (hupokhondriakós, “of the region between the ribs and navel”), from ὑποχόνδριος (hupokhóndrios, “the space between the ribs and the navel”), from ὑπό (hupó, “below”) + χόνδρος (khóndro
Learned borrowing from Late Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos, “river horse”).
From Late Latin hypothesis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (hupóthesis, “base, basis of an argument, supposition”).
From Late Latin homīlia.

parole.significato: to host (to perform the role of a host)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ospedar, from Late Latin hospitāre (or hospitor, hospitārī), from Latin hospes.
From Old Galician-Portuguese hospital, espital, spital, borrowed from Late Latin hospitālis (“hospice, shelter, guesthouse”), from Latin hospitālis (“hospitable”). Doublet of the inherited hospedal.

parole.significato: to humiliate, to injure dignity or self-respect
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese omillar (Cantigas de Santa Maria, 13th century); from Late Latin humiliāre, from humus (“ground, soil”). Compare Galician and Spanish humillar.

parole.significato: Hun (member of an ancient Turkic nomadic tribe)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin Hunnus, from Koine Greek Χοῦνοι (Khoûnoi) or Χουνοί (Khounoí), borrowed through Middle Iranian, apparently ultimately from Turkic *Hun-yü, the name of a tribe (they were known in China as Xiongnu). More at Huns.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin hallux, from Latin hallus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin hyphen, from Ancient Greek ὑφέν (huphén, “together”).

parole.significato: language (form of communication using words and structured with grammar)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin idioma, from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “peculiarity; idiom”).
Unknown. Perhaps from Late Latin iequāria, a derivative of iecur (“liver”); compare Old Spanish yegueria.
Borrowed from Late Latin illūminātiōnem, from Latin illūminō.
Borrowed from Late Latin immersiōnem.

parole.significato: impassive, impassible (having or revealing no emotion)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin impassibilis.
From Late Latin impeccābilis.
Borrowed from Late Latin imperturbābilis.
Borrowed from Late Latin impetuōsus. Compare Spanish impetuoso, French impétueux and Italian impetuoso.

parole.significato: impostor (someone who uses a false identity)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin impostōrem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin impostūra.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin inaccessibilis. By surface analysis, in- + acessível.
Modified, based on the Latin etymology, from Old Galician-Portuguese encensso, a semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin incēnsum, from Latin incēnsus.

parole.significato: to provide incentive, to incentivize; to foster, to encourage, to motivate
parole.testo: From incentivo + -ar, from Late Latin incentivum.
Borrowed from Late Latin incestuōsus.
Borrowed from Late Latin incīsiōnem.
Borrowed from Late Latin inconvenientia.

parole.significato: disbelief (unwillingness or inability to believe in something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin incrēdulitātem, from Latin incrēdulus.
Borrowed from Late Latin inculpāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin indicātōrem (“pointer”), from Latin indicō (“to point out”).
Borrowed from Late Latin indiscrētiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin indistīnctus. By surface analysis, in- + distinto.
Borrowed from Late Latin indūmentum (“garment”).
From Late Latin industriōsus.
Borrowed from Late Latin inductīvus, from Latin indūcō.

parole.significato: infallible (without fault or weakness; incapable of error or fallacy)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin īnfallibilis. By surface analysis, in- + falível.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin īnfanticīdium, from Latin īnfāns (“child”) + caedō (“to kill”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin iniectāre, injectāre, from Latin iniectus, injectus (compare iniciar).
Borrowed from Late Latin iniūriāre, from Latin iniūriārī.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin innovātiōnem. By surface analysis, inovar + -ção.

parole.significato: insatiable (incapable of being satisfied or appeased)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin īnsatiābilis.
Borrowed from Late Latin īnsēnsātus.

parole.significato: cold, tactless, undiplomatic, insensitive (not having normal emotional feelings)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin īnsēnsibilis. By surface analysis, in- + sensível.

parole.significato: inspiration (stimulating influence upon the intellect or emotions)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin īnspīrātiōnem, from Latin īnspīrō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin intellēctus, from Latin intellegō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin interruptōrem, from Latin interrumpō.

parole.significato: to entitle (give a title or name to)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin intitulāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin introductōrius, from Latin introductus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin intuitiōnem. Cognate with Galician and Spanish intuición and Catalan intuïció. By surface analysis, intuir + -ção.
Borrowed from Late Latin invāsiōnem (“attack, invasion”), from Latin invāsus (“entered, invaded”).

parole.significato: winter (the coldest of the four seasons)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese inverno~iverno, from Late Latin hībernum. For the added nasal in the first syllable, cf. Spanish invierno, etc.
Borrowed from Late Latin irrēgulāris.

parole.significato: European Portuguese standard spelling of irônico
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin īrōnicus, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός (eirōnikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin īrōnicus, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός (eirōnikós).

parole.significato: iterative (of a procedure that involves repetition)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin iterātīvus, from Latin iterātus.
Borrowed from Late Latin itinerantem.

parole.significato: to fast (to abstain from or eat very little food)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese jejũar, from Late Latin jejūnāre, alternative form of ieiūnāre, from Latin ieiūnus, from Proto-Indo-European *Hyeh₂ǵ-yu-.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese gẽolho, with metathesis, from Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu. Compare Galician xeonllo.
Borrowed from Late Latin Ioviālis.
Borrowed from Late Latin iūdaīzāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin iūdaismus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαϊσμός (Ioudaïsmós), from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yehuda, “Judah”).
From julgar (“to judge”) + -dor. Possibly corresponds to Late Latin jūdicātōrem or iūdicātōrem, accusative form of iūdicātor (“judger”), from Latin iūdicō.

From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Late Latin iūdicāmentum, from Latin iūdex (“judge”). By surface analysis, julgar + -mento. Compare Spanish juzgamiento, Catalan and Occitan jutjament, French jugement, Italian giudicamento.
From Old Galician-Portuguese juramento, from Late Latin iūrāmentum (“oath”), from Latin iūrō. By surface analysis, jurar + -mento.

parole.significato: to justify (provide an acceptable explanation for)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin iūstificāre. By surface analysis, justo + -ificar.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin iūstificātiōnem. By surface analysis, justificar + -ção.

parole.significato: lamprey (jawless eel-like fish of the class Petromyzontida)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin lampraeda, lamprēda. Cognate with Galician and Spanish lamprea, Italian lampreda, French lamproie, and English lamprey.

parole.significato: to spear (to pierce with a spear)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin lanceāre, from Latin lancea. Compare the inherited doublet lançar.
From Late Latin lanciārius, from Latin lancea + -ārius. By surface analysis, lança + -eiro.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lançar, from Late Latin lanceāre (“to throw a spear”), derived from Latin lancea (“spear”), from Celtiberian. Doublet of lancear and lança.
Inherited from Late Latin blastēmāre (variant of blasphēmāre). Doublet of blasfemar, which was borrowed from Latin.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin lavātōrium. By surface analysis, lavar + -tório Doublet of lavadouro, an alteration of the inherited lavadoiro.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin lēgislātiōnem (“the giving of the law”). By surface analysis, legislar + -ção.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin legibilis (“that can be read”).

parole.significato: milk (white liquid produced by the mammary glands)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese leite m, from Late Latin lactem m or f, from Latin lac n, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵlákts. Doublet of latte. Compare Galician leite m, Spanish leche f, Italian latte m and French lait m.
From Late Latin lēctūra, feminine of Classical Latin lēctūrus, from legō (“to read”). Compare Spanish and Catalan lectura.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin leopardus from Ancient Greek λεόπαρδος (leópardos) from λέων (léōn, “lion”) + πάρδος (párdos, “panther”).
Borrowed from Late Latin levisticum, probably an alteration of Latin ligusticum, from Ligusticus (“Ligurian”), ultimately from Ancient Greek Λίγυς (Lígus).

parole.significato: ligature (thread used to close a vessel or duct)
parole.testo: From Late Latin ligātūra.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ligātiōnem. By surface analysis, ligar + -ção. Compare Galician and Spanish ligazón, French liaison.

parole.significato: literal (understood exactly as written, without interpretation)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin litterālis.

parole.significato: litotes (an understatement employed for rhetoric effect)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin lītotēs, from Ancient Greek λιτότης (litótēs).
Borrowed from Late Latin locālis, from Latin locus. Cognate with the inherited lugar.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese logar, from Late Latin locālem (“local”), from Latin locus (“place”), from Latin stlocus, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put”). Compare Galician lugar, Fala lugal, Asturian llugar, and Spanish lugar. Doublet of local.
Borrowed from Late Latin lūmināria, neuter plural of lūmināre, from Latin lūmen.
From Old Galician-Portuguese luita, from Late Latin lucta, from Latin luctor. Compare Galician loita and Spanish lucha.

From Old Galician-Portuguese lampada, borrowed from Late Latin lampada, from Latin lampas, from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “lamp or flambeau”), from Ancient Greek λάμπω (lámpō, “to shine”). Compare the inherited Old Portuguese form lampaa.

parole.significato: legua, Portuguese league, a traditional unit of distance, variously reckoned as 4444.4, 5555.6, or 6172.8 m
parole.testo: From Late Latin leuga (“Gaulish league, the distance of one hour's walking”), from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *lougā. Cognate with Spanish and Galician legua and Catalan llegua.
From Old Galician-Portuguese *lendẽa, from Late Latin lendina, ultimately from Latin lendem. Compare Galician lendia.

parole.significato: logical (in agreement with the principles of logic)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin logicus.

parole.significato: stepmother (wife of one's biological father, not one's biological mother)
parole.testo: From Late Latin mātrastra (“stepmother”), from Latin māter (“mother”), from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr. Compare Galician madrasta, Spanish madrastra.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin magia, from Ancient Greek μαγεία (mageía).
From Late Latin malitātem, from Latin malus. By surface analysis, mal + -dade. Compare Spanish maldad.
From Late Latin malefactōrem, from Latin malefaciō. Compare French malfaiteur, Spanish malhechor.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mamar, from Late Latin mammō, from Latin mamma (“breast”) + -ō. By surface analysis, mama + -ar.
Possibly a derivative of Late Latin basilicum, from Ancient Greek βασιλικόν (basilikón).

From Old Galician-Portuguese manteer, mantẽer, from Late Latin manūtenēre (“to support”), from Latin manū (“with the hand”) + teneō (“to hold”). Compare Galician manter, Spanish mantener, French maintenir, Italian mantenere.

parole.significato: cloak (long outer garment worn over the shoulders covering the back)
parole.testo: From Late Latin mantum.
Variant of manufactura, from Late Latin manū factūra (“thing made by hand”).

parole.significato: to craft; to manufacture (to make something by hand)
parole.testo: Variant of manufacturar, from Late Latin manū factūra (“thing made by hand”).
Borrowed from Late Latin maniacus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μανιακός (maniakós), adjectival form of μανία (manía, “madness”). See mania.

parole.significato: material; stuff (the tangible substance that goes into the makeup of a physical object)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin māteriālis, from Latin māteria (“wood, material, substance”), from māter (“mother”). By surface analysis, matéria + -al.

parole.significato: enrolment (act of enrolling or state of being enrolled)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin mātrīcula, from Latin mātrīx.

From Old Galician-Portuguese maça, from Late Latin mattia or Vulgar Latin *mattea, probably from Latin mateola, from Proto-Indo-European *mat (“hoe, plow”). Compare Spanish maza, Italian mazza, Catalan maça, French masse.
From Late Latin mediāre, from Latin medius. Compare mediar (a borrowed doublet).
From Old Galician-Portuguese melanconia, borrowed from Late Latin melancholia, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía, “blackness of the bile”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós).

parole.significato: to improve, to ameliorate, to better
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese melhorar, from Late Latin meliōrāre, a verb based on Latin meliārī (“better”). Doublet of medrar.

parole.significato: Eurasian blackbird (A common true thrush, Turdus merula)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese melrro, from Late Latin merŭlum, from Latin merula.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese melon, from Late Latin mēlōnem, shortening of Latin mēlopepō, borrowed from Koine Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn).
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin mēnsuālis.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin mēnsūrāre.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin mēnsūrātiōnem, from Latin mēnsūra (“measurement”), from mētior (“measure”). By surface analysis, mensurar + -ção.
Borrowed from Late Latin mentālis, from Latin mēns. By surface analysis, mente + -al.

parole.significato: mixed (stemming from two or more races or breeds)
parole.testo: From Late Latin mixticius, from Latin mixtus (“mixed”). Compare Spanish mestizo, French métis.

parole.significato: half (one of two equal parts into which anything may be divided)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese metade displacing collateral form meiadade, from Late Latin medietātem (“center; midpoint”), from Latin medius (“middle; half”), from Proto-Indo-European *medʰyo- (“between”). Compare Spanish mitad.

From Late Latin metempsychosis, from Koine Greek μετεμψύχωσις (metempsúkhōsis), from μετεμψυχόομαι (metempsukhóomai, “of a soul, to pass from one body to another”), from μετα- (meta-) + ἐν (en, “in”) + ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”). By surface analysis, meta- + en- + psico- + -ose.

parole.significato: metonymy (the use of a single characteristic or name of an object to identify the entire object)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin metonymia, from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”), from μετά (metá, “other”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).

parole.significato: mine (place from which ore is extracted)
parole.testo: From Late Latin mīna, from Gaulish *mēnā (“ore, mine”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese minguar, from Late Latin minuāre, from Classical Latin minuere. Compare Galician minguar, Spanish menguar.

parole.significato: ministerial (related to a religious minister or ministry)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ministeriālis. By surface analysis, ministério + -al.

parole.significato: modern (pertaining to the current time and style)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin modernus; from Latin modo (“just now”).

parole.significato: mill (grinding apparatus or the building housing it)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese moinho, from Late Latin molīnum, from molīnus, from Latin molō. Compare Galician muíño, Spanish molino, French moulin, Catalan molí.

parole.significato: bundle (group of objects held together by wrapping or tying, especially keys or vegetables)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese mãollo, from Late Latin manuc(u)lus, modified ultimately from manipulus (“maniple; handful”), from manus (“hand”), from Proto-Indo-European *man-. Doublet of manolho and manojo. Compare Spanish manojo.
Borrowed from Late Latin monachālis.
Borrowed from Late Latin monarcha, from Ancient Greek μονάρχης (monárkhēs), variant of μόναρχος (mónarkhos, “sole ruler”).

parole.significato: monogamy (form of relationship in which an individual has only one partner during their lifetime or at any one time)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin monogamia, from Ancient Greek μονογαμία (monogamía). By surface analysis, mono- + -gamia.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin monosyllabicus, from Latin monosyllabus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek μονοσύλλαβος (monosúllabos). By surface analysis, mono- + silábico.
From Late Latin montāniōsus, an adjective based on montānia, from Latin montem (“mountain”). By surface analysis, montanha + -oso.
Borrowed from Late Latin monumentālis.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin monasticus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin monotonus, from Ancient Greek μονότονος (monótonos).

parole.significato: moratorium (authorization permitting temporary suspension of payments)
parole.testo: Feminine of moratório (“moratory”), from Late Latin morātōrium, neuter substantival use of Latin morātōrius (“delaying”), from moror (“to delay”), from mora (“delay”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese moordomo, mayordomo, from Late Latin maior domūs (“steward”), from Latin maior (“main, principal”) + genitive singular of domus (“household”).
Borrowed from Late Latin mūcōsus, from Latin mūcus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin mundānus, from Latin mundus (“world”).
Borrowed from Late Latin mundiālis.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin murmurium, from Latin murmur, from Proto-Indo-European *mormur-, *mur- (“to mutter”).
Inherited from Late Latin mutilātiōnem. Compare Galician and Spanish mutilación, Catalan mutilació, French mutilation, Italian mutilazione.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin multiplus.

parole.significato: nose (a protuberance on the face housing the nostrils, which are used to breathe or smell)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese nariz, from Late Latin nārīcem f, ultimately derived from Latin nāris. Compare Galician nariz m, Asturian, Aragonese, Ladino, and Spanish nariz f, Italian narice f.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin nāviculāris (“boat shaped”), from Latin nāvicula, diminutive of nāvis (“ship”), from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us.
From Old Galician-Portuguese nin (h)ũu, earlier nen (h)ũu, from Late Latin nec ūnus (“not even one”). Displaced the collateral form ningũu. Compare Galician ningún, Spanish ninguno.
From Old Galician-Portuguese neta, from Late Latin nepta, from Latin neptis (“granddaughter”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese neto, derived in masculine from the feminine neta, from Late Latin nepta, from Latin neptis (“granddaughter”).
From Late Latin (arbor) nucāria < nucārius < Latin nux. Compare Spanish noguera, French noyer, Catalan noguera, Occitan noguièr.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin nonna (“nun”).
Borrowed from Late Latin nosocomīum, from Ancient Greek νοσοκομεῖον (nosokomeîon, “hospital”), from νόσος (nósos, “disease, illness”) + κομέω (koméō, “to take care of”).

parole.significato: ball of rolled up thread or string
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese novelo, lovelo, from Late Latin lubellum < globellum, diminutive from Latin globus. Cf. Galician nobelo and Spanish ovillo.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese novembro, novenbro, from Late Latin Novembrius, from Latin November.

parole.significato: new moon (phase of moon when it is obscured)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin novilūnium.

parole.significato: novice (new member of a religious order)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese noviço, borrowed from Late Latin novīcius, novītius, from Latin novus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese nadega, from Late Latin natica, an adjectival term based on Latin natis (“rump, buttock”).

parole.significato: the (the definite grammatical article that shows that the noun phrase that immediately follows it is definitely identif…
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese o (compare Galician o), from Late Latin lo (compare Spanish lo) with loss of initial l, from earlier *illu, from Latin illum m, illud n, accusative singular forms of ille (“the”, “that”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin obnūbilātiōnem.

parole.significato: to work (to perform a work or labour)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin operāre, from Latin operārī. Doublet of operar, a borrowing.

parole.significato: offertory (part of the mass in which the priest offers the host and chalice)
parole.testo: From Late Latin offertorium, ultimately from Latin offerō. Compare Catalan and Spanish ofertorio, Italian offertorio.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin officiālis.
Borrowed from Late Latin oligarcha, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγάρχης (oligárkhēs).
Borrowed from Late Latin oligarchia, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχία (oligarkhía). By surface analysis, oligarca + -ia or oligo- + -arquia
Learned borrowing from Late Latin oligarchicus, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχικός (oligarkhikós). By surface analysis, oligarquia (“oligarchy”) + -ico (“-ic”, adjective-forming suffix).
Borrowed from Late Latin omissiōnem, from Latin omittō.
Formed based on Late Latin undula (“wavelet”), a diminutive of Latin unda (“wave”); corresponds to Medieval Latin undulāre. Cf. also ondulação.

parole.significato: onomatopoeia (property of a word of sounding like what it represents)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin onomatopoeïa, from Ancient Greek ὀνοματοποιία (onomatopoiía, “the coining of a word in imitation of a sound”).
Borrowed from Late Latin operārī. Doublet of obrar, which was inherited.
Inherited from Late Latin orificium.
Borrowed from Late Latin orīginārius.

Learned borrowing from Late Latin ūniōnem, from Latin ūnus (“one”).

parole.significato: to smear; to spread (to distribute in a thin layer)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese untar, from Late Latin unctāre, frequentative of Latin ungere (via its past participle unctus), from earlier unguere, from Proto-Italic *ongʷō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“anoint”).
From unto + -uoso, or borrowed from Late Latin unctuōsus, from Latin unctum.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ūnisonus (“having a single sound”).
Borrowed from Late Latin ūnivocus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese usofroyto, from Late Latin ūsufrūctus, from Latin ūsus et frūctus (“use and enjoyment”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese vagabondo, from Late Latin vagabundus, from Latin vagari (“wander”).

parole.significato: value (numerical quantity measured, assigned or computed)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese valor, from Late Latin valōrem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin valentia, from Latin valēns. By surface analysis, valer + -ência.

parole.significato: smallpox (an acute, highly infectious and often fatal disease)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin variola.

parole.significato: old; ancient (having existed for a long period of time)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese velho, from Late Latin veclus, from Latin vetulus.
Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin venēnōsus, from Latin venēnum. By surface analysis, veneno + -oso.
Borrowed from Late Latin veniālis, from Latin venia (“forgiveness”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ventilātiōnem, from Latin ventilō (“to brandish; to winnow”). By surface analysis, ventilar + -ção.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin verbālis. By surface analysis, verbo + -al.

From Old Galician-Portuguese verde (“green”), from Late Latin virdis, syncopated from Classical Latin viridis (“green”). Doublet of víride, which was borrowed from Latin. Cognate with Galician, Spanish, Italian, and Romanian verde, Catalan and Occitan verd, French vert and English vert, virid.
From Late Latin verticālis.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vilão, from Late Latin vīllānus (“farm worker”), from vīlla + -ānus. Cognate with Galician vilán and Spanish villano. By surface analysis, vila + -ão.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Late Latin vindicātōrem, from Latin vindicō. By surface analysis, vingar + -dor. Compare Spanish vengador.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin virtuōsus (“virtuous”), from Latin virtūs + -ōsus.
From Late Latin vīrulentus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wisós (“poison; slime; fluidity”).
Borrowed from Late Latin viscōsus, from Latin viscum. By surface analysis, visco + -oso.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin visuālis, from Latin visus.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vezinho, from Late Latin vēcīnus, from Latin vīcīnus. Compare Galician veciño, Spanish vecino.

parole.significato: vocabulary (set of words used by an individual)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin vocābulārium. By surface analysis, vocábulo + -ário.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin vulnerābilis. By surface analysis, vulnerar + -ável.

parole.significato: ethics (study of principles governing right and wrong conduct)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ethica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), feminine of ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).
From Late Latin indicum. Doublet of índico.
Inherited from Late Latin orphănus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos.

parole.significato: uvula (appendage that hangs from the palate)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin ūvula (“small grape”), diminutive of ūva.

From Old Galician-Portuguese abrigar, of disputed origin: most likely from Late Latin aprīcāre, from Latin aprīcārī (“to warm in the sun”), from aprīcus (“sunny”). Alternatively, and less likely, from Late Latin *abrīgāre (“to cover, shelter”), from a- + *brīgāre, from Frankish *birīhan (“to cover,

From Old Galician-Portuguese abrigo (“a place where one is sheltered from the elements or harm”), from abrigar, of disputed origin: possibly from Late Latin *abrīgāre (“to cover, shelter”), from a- + *brīgāre, from Frankish *biwrīhan (“to cover, protect”), from Proto-Germanic *bi- (“be-”) + *wrīhaną
From a- + longo + -ar, or from Vulgar Latin *allongāre, from Late Latin elongāre, from Latin longus.
From alvo + -ura, or from Late Latin albūra, from Latin albus.
Borrowed from Late Latin applānāre (“to flatten”), from Latin plānus. Doublet of achanar. Alternatively, from a- + plano + -ar. Compare with Spanish aplanar.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: From Dutch bakeljauw, bakkeljauw, of uncertain origin. Possibly from Late Latin baccalaureus, baculum (“stick, staff”), referring to the way cod were split and dried on wooden sticks. Or, possibly from Basque bakailao. The Basque term may be either the source or the descendant of Dutch kabeljauw, co

From Old Galician-Portuguese bufo, from Late Latin būfus (cognates include Spanish búho), itself either from Latin *būfō, from Faliscan *būfō, or more likely of onomatopoetic origin; cf. also Ancient Greek βοῦφος (boûphos). Compare to Latin būbō.
From Old Galician-Portuguese capitan, capitam, from Genoese Ligurian capitan, from Late Latin capitānus, from capitāneus, or from Latin capitālis.

parole.significato: rail (the metal bar that makes the track for a railroad)
parole.testo: From carro + -il, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *carrīlis, as an alteration of Late Latin currīlis, from Latin currus, with influence from carrus.
From comprar + -dor, or from Late Latin compārātōrem, from Latin compārō.
From Late Latin corrōsiō, corrōsiōnem, from corrōsus, perfect passive participle of corrōdō. Alternatively, from French corrosion.

From Old Galician-Portuguese cova, from Vulgar Latin *cova, from covus, alternative form of Latin cavus (or from a variant of Late Latin cava, from cavum, cavus), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱówHwos (“cavity”). Compare Spanish cueva.
From cravo + -ar, from Old Galician-Portuguese cravo (“nail”), from Latin clāvus (“nail”), or from Late Latin clāvāre, from Latin clāvus.

From Old Galician-Portuguese cambio, either directly from Late Latin cambium (“change”) or deverbal of cambiar (cf. Portuguese escambo), from Latin cambiāre (“to change”), from a Celtic language, from Proto-Celtic *kamb- (“crooked; bent”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱamb-, *(s)kamb- (“bent”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese descalço, from Vulgar Latin *discalceus, itself either from a shortening of discalceātus, from Late Latin discalceō, or from Latin dis- + calceus. Cognate with Galician and Spanish descalzo, Catalan descalç, Occitan descauç, French déchaux, Italian scalzo and Romanian de
From espinha + -al, or from Late Latin spīnālis, from Latin spīna.

parole.significato: to think that something is unusual or weird, to be surprised
parole.testo: From estranho (“strange/stranger”) + -ar. Alternatively, inherited from Late Latin extrāneāre, from Latin extrāneus. Compare Spanish extrañar, Galician and Asturian estrañar, Catalan estranyar.
Borrowed from Late Latin extēnsīvus, from Latin extēnsus. Alternatively, borrowed from French extensif, of the same Latin origins.

From falha, itself from a Vulgar Latin falla or falia (possibly partly through the intermediate or influence of Old French faille or Old Occitan), or from Old Galician-Portuguese fallar, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin fallāre, from Latin fallere.
From Old Galician-Portuguese falsar (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), either from Late Latin falsāre or a new verb formed on falso (“false”).

parole.significato: to horseshoe (to apply horseshoes to a horse or other hooved animal)
parole.testo: From ferro (“iron”) + -ar, or from a Late Latin ferrāre, from Latin ferrum (“iron”). Compare Spanish herrar, Catalan ferrar, French ferrer, Italian ferrare.
From lavandeiro (“launderer”), from Late Latin lavandārius, or from French lavandière. Compare also Spanish lavandera, Asturian llavandera.

parole.significato: to clean (to remove dirt from a place or object)
parole.testo: From limpo (“clean”) + -ar, or from Old Galician-Portuguese, from Late Latin limpidāre, from Latin limpidus (“clear; limpid”). Compare Spanish limpiar.

From Old Galician-Portuguese martelo, from Late Latin martellus, itself a diminutive of martulus, variant of Latin marculus, or alternatively based on malleus. Compare Galician martelo, Spanish martillo, Catalan martell, and Italian martello.

parole.significato: to mix (stir two or more substances together)
parole.testo: From mistura (“mixture”) + -ar (forms infinitives), from Latin mīxtura, feminine participle of misceō (“to mix”), from Proto-Indo-European *meiǵ-, *meiḱ- (“to mix”). Alternatively from Old Galician-Portuguese mesturar, from a Late Latin mixturāre, from Latin mīxtura. Compare Italian misturare, archa

parole.significato: wall (structure built for defence surrounding or separating an area)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian muraglia (“wall”), muro (“wall”) + -aglia, or from Late Latin muralia, from Latin mūrus.
From Old Portuguese ola + -eiro, or possibly from or Late Latin ollārius, from Latin ōlla.

parole.significato: jug with a capacity of approximately a litre
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pichel (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Old French pichier (“small jug”), from Late Latin pīcārium, alteration of bīcārium, itself possibly from bacarium, bacar or from Ancient Greek βῖκος (bîkos). Compare English pitcher; more at beaker.

parole.significato: pigsty (shelter or enclosure where pigs are kept)
parole.testo: From an Old Galician-Portuguese *porcilga, related to porco (“pig”), possibly through a Vulgar Latin *porcicula (with metathesis and later contraction), itself possibly from a crossing of Late Latin porcīle, from Latin porcus, and *cōrtīcula, diminutive of Latin cōrtem (“farmyard or enclosure”), or
From portar + -dor, or from Late Latin portātōrem, from Latin portō.
From Old Galician-Portuguese prova, either regressively derived from the verb provar or from Late Latin proba (“proof”), from Latin probō (“to approve; to prove”), from probus (“good”).
From queijo + -eiro, or from Late Latin cāseārius, from Latin cāseus. Compare Spanish quesero.

parole.significato: to bury, to cover in dirt, snow or rubble
parole.testo: From so- (“under”) + terra (“earth”) + -ar or possibly from Late Latin subterrāre, from Latin sub- + terra.

parole.significato: auger (tool for boring holes in wood)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese traado (13th century), from Late Latin taratrum (“auger”), attested by Isidore of Seville. Either from Paleo-Hispanic or from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *taratrom, from Proto-Indo-European *térh₁-tro-. Alternatively from Ancient Greek τέρετρον (téretron, “borer, gimlet”)

From Old Galician-Portuguese trõo, from trõar, or alternatively from Latin tonus (“thunderclap; sound, tone”), probably through a Late Latin or Vulgar Latin form *tronus, influenced by *tronitus < tonitrus. Compare Galician trono, Spanish trueno, Catalan tro, Occitan tron. See also tom, a possible d

parole.significato: to devotedly take care of something
parole.testo: From zelo (“zeal”) + -ar, or from Late Latin zēlāre, from Ancient Greek ζήλος (zḗlos, “zeal; jealousy”).
